query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated approach that couples high-throughput free‐energy simulations (via thermodynamic integration and metadynamics) with calibrated high-temperature differential scanning calorimetry and dilatometry can determine the melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys within ±10% error across a wide range of compositions.
generation.material_initial_state: Crystalline solid phase of high-entropy alloys before melting
generation.intervention: Application of integrated high-throughput free-energy simulations combined with high-temperature DSC and dilatometry calibration
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions near the melting point across diverse HEA compositions
generation.structural_mediator: The free-energy profile and calorimetric/dilatometric response during the solid-to-liquid transition that capture phase change phenomena
generation.mechanism: Advanced sampling methods calculate free-energy differences underlying phase transitions while calibrated calorimetry and dilatometry translate these into precise thermodynamic property measurements, ensuring that latent heat, entropy changes, and volume modifications are accurately captured.
generation.predicted_outcome: For a broad set of high-entropy alloys, the integrated method will yield melting temperatures, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change measurements that agree with baseline techniques within an error margin of approximately ±10%, while significantly reducing experimental and computational resource requirements.
generation.baseline: Traditional CALPHAD assessments, stand-alone high-temperature calorimetry, and independent atomistic simulation methods
generation.boundary: This approach may be less reliable in alloys exhibiting extreme atomic size mismatches or unexpected contaminant phases, where interatomic potentials and experimental calibrations may fail.
generation.uncertainty: While the integrated method is theoretically promising, the precise quantitative error bounds and efficiency gains across the full HEA compositional space need systematic benchmarking.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative set of high-entropy alloys covering a broad compositional range. Apply the integrated high-throughput free-energy/DSC/dilatometry method to measure melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting. Compare these measurements with those obtained from established baseline methods. Statistical analysis will determine if deviations exceed the ±10% error threshold.
measurements: Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties (e.g., specific heat, viscosity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, in more than 40% of the tested alloy compositions, the integrated method's values deviate by more than ±10% from the benchmark values, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The extremely harsh environment of the high temperature plasma imposes strict requirements on the construction materials of the first wall in a fusion reactor. In this work, a refractory alloy system, WTaVTiZrx, with low activation and high entropy, was theoretically designed based on semi-empirical formula and produced using a laser cladding method. The effects of Zr proportions on the metallographic microstructure, phase composition, and alloy chemistry of a high-entropy alloy cladding layer were investigated using a metallographic microscope, XRD (X-ray diffraction), SEM (scanning electron microscope), and EDS (energy dispersive spectrometer), respectively. The high-entropy alloys have a single-phase BCC structure, and the cladding layers exhibit a typical dendritic microstructure feature. The evolution of microstructure and mechanical properties of the high-entropy alloys, with respect to annealing temperature, was studied to reveal the performance stability of the alloy at a high temperature. The X-ray diffraction analyzer (XRD, D/MAX 2500 V) is employed for phase analysis of the sample prepared in this experiment. The experiment utilized Cu target Kα (λ = 0.154056 nm), with a voltage of 40 KV and a current of 40 mA. The scanning rate was set to 2°/min, the scanning angle range is between 10° and 100°. As there exists a one-to-one correspondence between each crystalline material and its diffraction pattern, this experiment combined XRD spectra with Jade 6 analysis software to determine the phase composition and crystal structure of the alloy sample. To investigate the high temperature softening resistance of the WTaVTiZr high-entropy alloy, vacuum annealing was performed on original samples and annealed samples at 900 °C, 1100 °C, and 1200 °C for 5 h and 10 h using a muffle furnace and vacuum sealing techniques. The SEM, EDS, XRD, and microhardness results of the original samples and vacuum annealing samples at different temperatures and times were compared to study the high-temperature anti-softening performance and phase structure stability of this high-entropy alloy composition.

AbstractHigh‐performance soft magnetic materials are important for energy conservation and emission reduction. One challenge is achieving a combination of reliable temperature stability, high resistivity, high Curie temperature, and high saturation magnetization in a single material, which often comes at the expense of intrinsic coercivity–a typical trade‐off in the family of soft magnetic materials with homogeneous microstructures. Herein, a nanostructured FeCoNiSiAl complex concentrated alloy is developed through a hierarchical structure strategy. This alloy exhibits superior soft magnetic properties up to 897 K, maintaining an ultra‐low intrinsic coercivity (13.6 A m−1 at 297 K) over a wide temperature range, a high resistivity (138.08 µΩ cm−1 at 297 K) and the saturation magnetization with only a 16.7% attenuation at 897 K. These unusual property combinations are attributed to the dual‐magnetic‐state nature with exchange softening due to continuous crystal ordering fluctuations at the atomic scale. The third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure Cr and V in both the liquid and A2 phases were established. By applying these expressions, the thermodynamic properties down to 0 K and thermal vacancy near the melting point can be well described. Besides, the lattice stability of Cr and V over the whole temperature range can be guaranteed. Based on the third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure elements, the Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were thermodynamically assessed by considering the reviewed phase equilibria and thermodynamic data with the CALPHAD approach. A strategy to estimate the Gibbs energy of Laves phase was proposed by combining the theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic properties as well as semiempirical relation. Such a method was applied to C14 and C15 Laves phases in Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems. The calculated phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties showed nice agreement with the measured ones. Significant improvements can be observed at low temperatures compared with those from the second-generation thermodynamic descriptions, indicating the high reliability of the present thermodynamic descriptions.

frame.system: High-entropy alloys – multi‐principal element alloy systems that are typically processed from a solid state and then melted; the starting state is the crystalline solid phase before fusion.
frame.goal: To develop a method that accurately and efficiently determines melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the entire compositional range of high-entropy alloys.
frame.limitation: Existing approaches either lack accuracy or efficiency when applied to the vast, complex compositional space of high-entropy alloys, and may have limited ranges of applicability or insufficient physical grounding across all relevant melting phenomena.

decision.trend: Early HEA studies mostly concentrated on structure and mechanical properties, with initial works (e.g., PMC4740901) focusing on the crystalline solid state and later ones (e.g., PMC8320920) innovating in imaging the melting process in situ via neutron radiography. CALPHAD, atomistic simulations, and calorimetric techniques were developed to approximate phase evolution and thermal behaviors; however, these methods suffered from either limited extrapolation in complex alloy spaces or high computational/experimental costs. Researchers gradually moved from qualitative or isolated measurements of Melting phenomena toward approaches leveraging advanced sampling techniques and integrated measurements, but a method capturing all key melting thermodynamic properties across the full compositional space remains elusive.
decision.unsolved: A method that combines high accuracy (with quantitative error bounds) and efficiency for determining melting temperature, latent heats (fusion enthalpy and entropy), volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamics across the full range of high-entropy alloys is still missing. Existing methods either do not cover the extreme compositional variability or do not capture all aspects of the melting process in a physically rigorous way.
decision.lever: integrated high-throughput free-energy simulations using techniques such as thermodynamic integration/metadynamics combined with calibrated high-temperature differential scanning calorimetry and dilatometry
decision.why: This approach directly addresses the unsolved challenge by combining advanced sampling, which has proven effective in capturing free-energy differences with explicit error bounds, with experimental validation under controlled alloy composition and temperature settings. It builds on the successful trend of in situ characterization (as seen in PMC8320920) and the push towards integrating computational and experimental methods to achieve accurate, efficient, and universally applicable predictions across the high-entropy-alloy family.
